The 82% cap stands for exactly the reason it was set.

hypotheses.name: The Iran file is coalition-captured (the capture read, tracked as opinion)
hypotheses.d: The claim: on the Iran file, organized coalition pressure — donor networks, primary structure, allied commitments, defense-institutional momentum — outweighs the base's war fatigue, which is why a 'no more wars' White House struck anyway and now substitutes sanctions for settlement rather than sign a visible retreat before the midterms. Mechanisms named, plural: status clock vs electoral clock, sunk cost after declaring victory, lobbies as veto players that raise the price of defection (one interest group among several — any single-key version of this hypothesis is scored separately and currently rejected). Held at 70%: the strike itself, the 6-month grind, and 'not in a hurry' all fit; capped because the same facts also fit ordinary planning failure plus vanity. Falsifier: a signed de-escalation or negotiated Hormuz reopening BEFORE the midterms — the base's clock winning on the party's most captured file would kill the strong form outright.

hypotheses.name: Nobody's hurrying on Hormuz — 60% → 65% (RAISED)
hypotheses.d: Its first fact that BEATS a rival instead of merely fitting itself. On 30 Aug the US struck two IRGC rocket launchers on Larak after observing Guard personnel preparing to fire rockets carrying sea mines into the strait — two days after CENTCOM declared the lanes fully cleared, and while Muscat negotiates a minesweeping calendar. The 08-30 audit had installed a genuine rival — a physical clock, minesweeping simply takes time — and ruled this hypothesis must beat it. A physical clock runs down; this one is being rewound, by the exact actor the hypothesis named in advance. Capped at +5 on three counts kept in front: CENTCOM is the interested party and 'observed preparations' is unpublished intelligence used to justify a strike; Al Jazeera published a technical challenge on 31 Aug to whether Iran can even mine by rocket as claimed; and IRGC counter-coercion against a blockade that has redirected 83 vessels, disabled three and boarded two explains the same act without any rent motive. Not pre-event.

hypotheses.name: Détente as harvest cover — HELD 60%, tell sharpened
hypotheses.d: August continues the signature: 125 PLA aerial ADIZ incursions (the 2026 decline intact) against 152 non-warship PRC vessels in the first 21 days, ~60% coast guard, with the east-of-Taiwan patrols now a declared 'new normal'. Kinetic down, jurisdiction up. NOT moved — this is the same signal that bought +5 on 08-26, and re-marking on the continuation of its own evidence is the double-count the audit named. The important item is against my own test: if Beijing has DECLARED the patrols permanent, their persistence through the Sept 24 visit is close to uninformative. Re-specified now, in advance and stricter — the informative observation on 09-23→09-25 is a boarding, an inspection, or a first-time-area incursion. Mere presence no longer counts as confirmation.

hypotheses.name: Venezuela was a Hormuz hedge in a drug-war uniform
hypotheses.d: The clearest revealed-preference play on the board — and the reason it holds at 55 rather than higher. Sturdy mechanism first: US Gulf-Coast refineries are plumbed for heavy sour crude, Venezuela sits on the planet's largest heavy reserves, and moving that barrel north through the Caribbean to Texas and Louisiana structurally hedges the one risk that ran live all year — a Hormuz closure. The Aug 28-29 deal (a new operator taking control of ~65bn barrels, about a fifth of Venezuela's reserves) is exactly what this hypothesis predicts. So oil-as-motive is near-certain. What is NOT settled — and what caps this — is premeditation: was Southern Spear a counter-narcotics and regime-change campaign that harvested the oil after the fact, or an oil-security operation in a drug-war uniform from the start? The tell against design is the clock — the deal trailed Maduro's Jan 3 capture by eight months, which reads more like spoils than master plan. Falsifiers: token export volumes, Gulf-Coast heavy sourcing not actually swinging off the Middle East, or the fixed infrastructure (GEO-022) never appearing. One correction the excitement needs: a canal cannot bypass Hormuz — the hedge is source substitution plus Caribbean routing, not a waterway. Note it is DISTINCT from 'The Portfolio State' below, which is about the vehicle rather than the motive.

hypotheses.name: US drift hardened into leverage play — HELD 52%
hypotheses.d: Confirming but shared, therefore ambience: Treasury again held back on Chinese financial institutions, with mainstream reporting now naming the mechanism outright — designating them 'could create tensions before Xi's visit'. Bessent's promised weekly cadence hit banks but no Chinese one, and at the G20 he pushed severing Iran financial ties while China dissented. Both the leverage read and the ordinary 'Washington won't detonate its own summit' read predict all of it. The strongest weekly argument AGAINST, logged rather than absorbed: the US struck Iran on three consecutive nights and took Iranian fire onto three Arab host states. Deliberate slow-walking for leverage sits badly with sustained kinetic escalation that raises the cost of the thing being slow-walked — that counterweight is what holds the number at 52.

hypotheses.name: A pre-announcement leak into oil futures — 40% → 34% (biggest mover)
hypotheses.d: Its lead conditional has now gone unfired across three weeks containing the most violently market-moving Iran news since April — the 30 Aug Larak strike, three nights of exchanges, two struck VLCCs, Brent to ~$95 — with not one reported nine-figure pre-announcement episode. The file is confirmed as historical and bounded: DOJ is probing four trades totalling ~$2.6bn, all inside a five-week window that closed in April — Mar 23 (>$500m, ~15 min before Trump's delay post), Apr 7 ($960m before the ceasefire), Apr 17 ($760m, ~20 min before Iran said Hormuz was open), Apr 21 ($430m before the extension). CORRECTION BANKED AGAINST THIS ENTRY: the ledger's earlier '~$2.2bn cluster' for Mar 23 and its '~$7bn' aggregate are both withdrawn as over-wide constructions. The cut is made on the hypothesis's own written terms, not on a preferred reading — a conditional set at 60% has burned three of fourteen weeks in the best environment it will ever get and produced nothing. The cut is only −6 because of one genuinely new structural fact: investigators are running a SEPARATE probe into prediction-market activity on the same developments, and the same foreknowledge reaching two unrelated venues is hard to explain as one market-maker hedging client flow. Split now: deliberate leak 34 / mediator-side 20 / skilled opportunism 36 / coincidence 10. Still the only entry whose evidence is timestamped BEFORE the event.

hypotheses.name: NEW · The Portfolio State — coercion converted into sovereign equity, statute retrofitted
hypotheses.d: Strongest form: the US is converting military and sanctions leverage into permanent state equity in strategic supply chains, with the legal authority written to fit transactions rather than the reverse — Venezuela being the first hydrocarbon use of a template already run in chips and critical minerals. The rail predates the headline, which is the only thing licensing a design read at all: Senate NDAA FY2027 §1051 was marked up in MID-JUNE — ten weeks before the 29 Aug deal — creating a DoD Equity Investment Account, authorising OSC equity to $500m and capping any single position at 40% of the entity; the Venezuela stake is 35%, inside a cap that does not legally exist yet. Add DoD's own $400m/15% stake in MP Materials with 100% offtake (structurally identical to Venezuela's '20% of output at cost'), House Oversight already demanding an accounting of Venezuelan oil revenue on 23 Feb, and CFR's tally of 26 government equity deals worth ~$23.9bn. It opens at only 25% because the boring, incompetence and patronage readings are all strong: think tanks have been publicly naming and counting this pattern since 2025 (a policy, not a plot); the Pentagon's own spokesman flatly DENIES that OSC takes equity while WSJ reports it doing so, which is improvisation not design; and a 100-year concession over 65bn bbl routed to one politically connected operator with no published contract is better explained as spoils allocation. Above all the base rate is enormous — Anglo-Persian 1914, the RFC, GM/Chrysler 2009 — so the design premium must be small. NOT a conspiracy claim and must never be scored as one: it requires no secrecy at all, only anticipation, and the honest gap is that I cannot name the operator who executes the warrants. Key test: does the ENACTED NDAA widen §1051 beyond critical minerals to energy, or raise the cap, by 31 Dec (45%)? Scope enacted unchanged kills the design read.

hypotheses.name: Moscow shapes Tehran's maximalism — 25% → 22% (CUT, sixth session running)
hypotheses.d: The week finally produced Russia-Iran material and it is the wrong KIND. Moscow said publicly on 01 Sep that air defence is the main focus of military-technical cooperation with Iran, alongside a reported 500 Verba MANPADS and 2,500 missiles and continued fighter deliveries. That is the resupply leg — already priced at 7/10 under 'means'. It moves nothing: it is announced by TASS, an interested party publishing its own helpfulness and the structural opposite of a covert channel; the opportunism branch predicts arms sales to a client at war identically, so under the standing rule it is ambience; and after six sessions there is still ZERO documentary evidence Moscow has influenced Tehran's negotiating position, which is the actual claim. Arms transfers are not persuasion. Cut rather than held because a decay rule that bites only on its deadline is a cliff, not decay. Clock unchanged: 15% on 30 Sep absent documentary evidence, retire below 10%.

hypotheses.name: War pause was secretly packaged with the Beijing summit — on the retirement line
hypotheses.d: Nothing resolved this week, and one file addition cuts against it: the summit's Iran content is now openly reported as an explicit US ask — Chinese pressure on Tehran to reopen the strait — with Beijing expected to want Taiwan concessions in return. An openly negotiated Iran-for-Taiwan trade is this hypothesis's RIVAL, not its confirmation; the secret-package version needs the deal hidden, and the deal is being conducted in headlines. Retirement trigger unchanged; the test runs on schedule on 24 Sept.

brief.head: Houthi drones and missiles hit four Saudi cities, wounding 73
brief.h: Iran-aligned Houthi forces struck a coalition airbase at Khamis Mushait and Saudi Aramco sites at Abha, Najran and Jazan with drones and ballistic missiles on Tuesday, wounding 73 people including women and children, halting operations at some energy facilities and pushing Brent to $99.22 - its highest since 24 July - hours after a Saudi-led coalition airstrike cratered the runway at Sanaa airport to stop an aircraft arriving from Tehran.
brief.t: Read the trigger before the damage, because the coverage mostly buried it. This wave answers a strike on the Sanaa runway that blocked a flight from Tehran, which means the fight is about the eleven-year air and naval blockade of Yemen - oil is simply the address at which Riyadh can be invoiced. The specific asset that converts a Yemeni grievance into a global price is the Jazan complex: 400,000 barrels a day, roughly a tenth of Aramco's net refining capacity, already shut twice since late July and restarted late on 30 August. That matters because the world is short conversion capacity, not crude. And note what the Saudi energy ministry did not say - nothing about crude exports, which load at Ras Tanura and Yanbu, hundreds of miles from anything hit today. The market bought a refining story and priced it as a supply story.
brief.context: R0 dates this to E4, the 1973 security-for-barrels bargain in which Washington guarantees the Gulf's airspace and Riyadh guarantees the barrel. The rail is older than the headline: the coalition blockade of Yemen has run since 2015, and Iran already struck Saudi Arabia directly between February and June this year, hitting Ras Tanura and Prince Sultan Air Base - so this is a reopened front, not a new one. The desk that decides is not CENTCOM but Aramco's outage schedule and the war-risk underwriters who quote southern Red Sea calls, because repair time and insurance rates set the price long after the fires are out. The base rate that governs the escalation question is Abqaiq, September 2019: 5.7 million barrels a day off line, half the kingdom's output, attributed by Washington to Iran directly - and no American strike on Iran followed, only a troop deployment and a sanctions round. That is why this board HELD its Iran-campaign forecast at 51 per cent today rather than raising it. The influence map runs Houthi command as agent, Tehran as principal-by-supply, Riyadh as the target paying in repair bills, and the diesel crack as the market pricing the coercion. Falsifier, dated: if a Houthi strike lands on a crude EXPORT terminal - Ras Tanura, Yanbu, or the Jazan marine terminal rather than its refinery - before 31 December, the 'taxing the refinery, not ending the export' read is wrong and this board must say so.

consp.claim: That the Houthis are the named author but not the actual shooter - that drones and ballistic missiles reaching Abha, Khamis Mushait and Najran with this accuracy imply Iranian targeting support, and that the Houthi claim is a deniability wrapper letting Tehran hit Saudi Arabia without owning the strike.
consp.spread: Loud on Gulf-security and OSINT accounts on X and in Reddit's geopolitics threads within hours of the first fires, almost always framed as 'remember Abqaiq'.
consp.read: This maps onto a documented precedent rather than a fantasy, which is why it deserves serious handling: UN monitors concluded in 2020 that the Houthis did NOT carry out the 2019 Abqaiq attack despite claiming it, because the weapons lacked the range and the facilities were approached from the north rather than from Yemen in the south. The checkable kernel is geometry and debris - impact bearings and recovered airframes - and it resolves in weeks, not never. It is downstream of a real structural feature of proxy war: the sponsor buys deniability, the proxy buys prestige, and both have an incentive to leave authorship ambiguous. One honest difference from 2019, though: Abha and Najran sit on the Yemeni border and are comfortably within Houthi range, so the range argument that broke the 2019 claim does not obviously transfer to today's targets.

angles.party: Traders long the front of the oil curve
angles.effect: gain - a $2 move on a refining and casualty event that touched no export barrel
pay - repair costs, 73 wounded, and a fourth disruption at Jazan in six weeks at a plant already restarted late
gains - a blockade grievance converted into a world price, the cheapest publicity a non-state actor can buy

angles.party: Diesel buyers: hauliers, farmers, shipping lines
angles.effect: pay - the crack widens because conversion capacity, not crude, is the binding constraint

dec.kill: Saudi crude export loadings from Ras Tanura and Yanbu. If they hold at recent volumes over the next fortnight, today was a refining and casualty event that the market priced as a supply event.

brief.head: Russia fires 166 drones hours after the Kyiv pause runs out
brief.h: Ukraine's air force counted 166 drones and 32 cruise missiles plus ballistic and anti-ship rounds overnight, killing two in Kyiv and five nationwide with 63 wounded, hours after the 72-hour capitals truce covering Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner's Moscow-and-Kyiv shuttle expired - with Zelenskyy saying talks are possible this month but the war will run into winter.
brief.t: The informative fact is not the barrage, it is the timing precision. A pause that begins when envoys land and ends when they leave is not a step toward a ceasefire; it is a scheduling accommodation, and it demonstrates that Moscow can switch the air campaign on and off at will - which is an argument for its confidence, not its exhaustion. Follow what each party actually bought: Washington got a photograph of two capitals quiet at once, Kyiv got 72 hours of sleep, and Moscow got to establish that the quiet is a gift it owns and can withdraw. Zelenskyy's own summary - talks perhaps this month, war into the winter - is the honest description of a negotiation in which neither side has yet paid anything that would be expensive to reverse.
brief.context: The rail is the Korean armistice template, which is why this board carries a separate conditional at 85 per cent that any stop to this war arrives as an armistice without a peace treaty. The desk that decides is not the envoys but the Russian General Staff's strike-planning cycle and Ukraine's interceptor inventory - an air truce is an ammunition arrangement before it is a political one. Virginia Page Fortna's work on ceasefire durability is the framework doing the work: ceasefires without monitors, guarantors or a demilitarised separation fail at high rates, and nothing announced this week contains any of the three. The base rate is that brief diplomatic pauses convert into durable ceasefires only rarely and almost never without third-party guarantees, which is why this board CUT its 30-day-ceasefire forecast from 20 to 18 today rather than reading the pause as progress. This also closes a falsifier we published in advance on 09-06 - it said the lapse would be informative if it came with no extension and no jointly acknowledged text, and that is precisely what happened, so the cut is a scored result rather than a reaction. The next falsifier is equally cheap to check: a jointly acknowledged document, containing a demarcation line or a monitoring mechanism, confirmed by both capitals before 31 October. Absent that, 'substantive' is an adjective.

consp.claim: That the peace track is a deal-making franchise rather than diplomacy - that Witkoff and Kushner are negotiating reconstruction and investment access with Moscow under a peace label, with the $2bn Affinity Partners received from Saudi Arabia's sovereign fund and the $2bn UAE-backed investment into World Liberty Financial's stablecoin offered as the motive.
consp.spread: Broad and unusually cross-partisan: Democratic senators have made it a formal conflict-of-interest complaint, Republican Senator Thom Tillis said the pairing 'doesn't make any sense', and pro-administration forums run a mirror version in which the two are the only honest brokers precisely because they are not State Department careerists.
consp.read: The frame is foreign policy as private dealmaking, and its checkable kernel is narrow but real - the investments are publicly reported and neither envoy went through Senate confirmation, so the ordinary financial-disclosure machinery never ran. What that does not establish is causation, that the money shaped a negotiating position. The boring alternative covers most of the evidence: a president who trusts two people, distrusts the institutional bureaucracy and wants an announceable deal produces exactly this staffing whether or not anyone's fund benefits.

brief.head: China's exports jump 25pc weeks before Xi meets Trump
brief.h: August exports rose 25 per cent year on year on semiconductors, computing hardware and autos, widening the monthly trade surplus to $119.1bn from $112.5bn and taking the year-to-date surplus to $805.5bn, with shipments to the United States up 34.4 per cent - even as both governments explore reciprocal tariff cuts on $30bn of goods each ahead of the state visit.
brief.t: Two numbers point in opposite directions and it matters which one is actually new. A record surplus is not news - China ran $1.2 trillion last year and the structure that produces it has not changed. What is new is a live, numbered de-escalation: $30bn of reciprocal cuts under negotiation sixteen days before a summit is the most concrete thing the tariff file has produced since the May truce. Then follow the composition rather than the headline. The surge is in AI-adjacent hardware - chips, servers, the machinery of the datacentre build-out - which means American demand for Chinese exports is now being pulled by the one sector Washington least wants to depend on. That is leverage moving the wrong way for the US position, and it is why this board cut its truce-collapse forecast to 18 per cent: a country importing what it needs is a country that renews.
brief.context: R0 places this in E5, the post-2001 WTO accession rail, in its late chapter where the tariff wall is high and the flows route around it. The desk that decides is USTR's exclusion process and Commerce's entity list, not the podium - tariff schedules are administered, not announced, and the administrative layer is where a truce actually lives or dies. The framework is Farrell and Newman on weaponised interdependence: chokepoints bite when a flow must pass a node you control, and consumer electronics do not, which is why tariffs have moved the ROUTE of Chinese goods more than the volume. The base rate is the discipline here - negotiated trade truces between major partners are renewed far more often than they collapse, because both sides have already paid the political cost of the deal once and neither wants to pay it again in an election year. The falsifier is publishable and dated: if Washington publishes the 7.5 per cent overcapacity finding, or adds a top-ten Chinese bank to the SDN list, before 24 September, the truce-collapse question deserves a sharp raise rather than a two-point cut.

consp.claim: That the surplus is partly fictional - that a large share of what registers as Chinese and Vietnamese exports is the same goods relabelled to dodge tariffs, so the official numbers on both sides are measuring paperwork rather than production.
consp.spread: No longer fringe: the White House's own Office of Trade and Manufacturing Policy published a report titled 'The Great Transshipment Scam' costing it at up to $303bn across 40 jurisdictions, and a harder version circulates on trade-focused X and in economics subreddits holding that most of the surplus is laundering.
consp.read: This is the rare case where the establishment version is the loud one and the academic version is the deflating one. Researchers at Harvard, Duke and Academia Sinica found roughly $8bn of Chinese exports rerouted through Vietnam in the first three quarters of 2025 - real, and small against a trillion-dollar aggregate. The estimate also collapses as the matching tightens: about 16.5 per cent of US-bound Vietnamese exports look rerouted at the national product level, 6.5 per cent when matched within provinces, and 1.7 per cent within individual firms. Aggregation is doing most of the work in the big number, and the checkable kernel - firm-level customs matching - already exists.

angles.effect: gains - a $303bn figure justifies extending tariffs to third countries without opening a new front with Beijing
pay - they absorb tariffs and audits for flows that firm-level data suggest are overwhelmingly their own production
pay either way - August's surge is concentrated in exactly the goods American datacentres are buying
gain - every month the surplus prints high while a reciprocal cut is being drafted improves their hand

dec.kill: Firm-level rather than product-level customs matching applied to 2026 data. If the within-firm rerouting rate stays near 1.7 per cent, the 'the surplus is laundering' claim is measuring aggregation, not fraud.

brief.head: Twelve countries ban trade with Israeli West Bank settlements
brief.h: Britain, France and Canada announced a twelve-country restriction on goods from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank - joined by Denmark, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Poland, Portugal and Sweden - citing settlement expansion and the E1 project near Jerusalem, with the UK's own measure taking up to nine months to come into force, Bezalel Smotrich demanding the British ambassador's expulsion and President Herzog calling it 'a grave miscalculation'.
brief.t: Measure this one by weight rather than by volume. Settlement goods are overwhelmingly agricultural - fresh produce and wine - and a rounding error in Israel's total trade, so the economic bite is close to nothing and every party involved knows it. What is actually being built is a legal distinction: twelve states formally separating settlement goods from Israeli goods creates customs categories, rules-of-origin tests and a compliance apparatus that outlives whichever government created it. Categories are cheap to build and expensive to dismantle, which is the real mechanism here. The nine-month implementation window is the tell in the other direction - a signal calibrated to remain reversible if Washington objects.
brief.context: The rail predates the headline by a decade. The EU's 2015 interpretive notice on labelling settlement produce and the 2019 Psagot judgment at the European Court of Justice already built the machinery for distinguishing settlement origin, so today is a permit exercised on an existing statute rather than a new instrument - which is exactly the pattern that licenses a design read. The deciding desk is the customs authority and the rules-of-origin officer, not the foreign ministry that held the press conference. Nicholas Mulder's history of the interwar economic weapon supplies the framework: coercion works through the leakage path, and the leakage path here is enormous - the American market is untouched, the goods are fungible, and re-export through Israel proper is trivially available. The base rate for narrow product bans changing a settlement policy is close to zero; what such measures historically change is the defending state's legal exposure in later litigation. The falsifier is dated: if any of the twelve extends the measure from settlement goods to Israeli financial or defence transactions before 31 March 2027, this was the opening move of a sanctions campaign rather than a labelling exercise.

consp.claim: That the twelve-country announcement was timed to swing Israel's late-October election - that a coordinated multi-state trade action landing seven weeks before a vote is campaign intervention wearing a customs uniform.
consp.spread: This one is not anonymous: Israeli President Isaac Herzog accused Britain outright of interfering in the coming election, and the claim then ran hard through Israeli political accounts and US conservative media, amplified by Ambassador Mike Huckabee calling the measure 'discrimination against the Jewish people' and warning of American 'repercussions or retaliations'. A mirror version circulates on the other side holding that Herzog's interference charge is itself the campaign move.
consp.read: The timing claim has a real kernel and a checkable one: the vote is due in late October, the measure lands now, and the UK's own implementation window runs up to nine months - so nothing binds before Israelis vote, which is either evidence of a signal aimed at the campaign or evidence that it was deliberately built to bite nobody. The frame it maps onto is 'foreign pressure as election meddling', a claim every incumbent under external sanction reaches for, and its analytic weakness is that it predicts the same thing whatever the calendar says. The boring alternative is stronger: twelve governments moved when their own domestic coalitions demanded a visible action, and European legislative calendars, not Israeli ones, set the date.

angles.effect: gain - a visible, low-cost action for domestic constituencies demanding pressure, with no security or intelligence relationship touched
pay - a real if small market loss concentrated on a few thousand growers
gain politically - Smotrich and Ben-Gvir get a foreign adversary to campaign against, which is why the response was expulsion demands rather than negotiation

angles.party: Palestinian residents of the West Bank
angles.effect: gain nothing measurable - the E1 project cited as the trigger is entirely unaffected by a produce ban

dec.kill: Whether E1 construction tenders proceed on schedule. If they do, the ban changed the label on the crate and nothing on the ground.

brief.head: UK 30-year yield hits 5.89pc, its highest since 1998
brief.h: Britain paid its steepest thirty-year borrowing rate since 1998 at Tuesday's gilt sale, the long yield reaching 5.89 per cent, as war-driven inflation expectations, heavy long-dated corporate issuance from technology borrowers and doubts about the October Budget collided - while the Treasury bench insisted on 'fiscal credibility'.
brief.t: This is the leg of the curve that no monetary innovation repairs, and it is worth being precise about why. Stablecoins and the Fed's standing bill programme manufacture demand for SHORT paper - bills, not thirty-year bonds - so the more the dollar plumbing is rebuilt around tokenised claims, the more the bid concentrates at the front while the long end is left to pension funds, insurers and price-sensitive foreigners. Now follow the money into the auction: with Brent at $99 and an energy-driven inflation term embedded in every long forecast, a thirty-year buyer is being asked to guess the average inflation rate out to 2056 during a war over the world's main oil chokepoint. They are charging 5.89 per cent for the guess. That is not a British story with a Gulf footnote; it is a Gulf story arriving as a British invoice.
brief.context: R0 dates this to E6, the 2008-2022 quantitative-easing rail in its unwind chapter: the central bank that was the price-insensitive marginal buyer of long duration is now a seller, and the private buyers who replaced it price risk properly. The desk that decides is the Debt Management Office's issuance calendar and the liability-driven positioning of UK pension funds, not the Bank of England's policy rate, which reaches the short end. The 2022 Truss episode is the base rate and the right one to reach for, with the difference named honestly: 2022 was a solvency scare triggered by an unfunded fiscal announcement, transmitted through LDI margin calls, and it moved in days. This is a grind, driven by supply and inflation expectations, and grinds historically resolve through slower fiscal adjustment rather than through a gilt crisis. This board's own money-printer red board reads YELLOW today with two of four live lines crossed - the US ten-year at 4.77 above its 4.75 threshold and Brent above $91 - and it is worth publishing against our own convenience that the board's gilt line is a lagged monthly series reading 4.80 per cent, which cannot see today's 5.89. The falsifier for the calm read: a failed or heavily tailed gilt auction, or Bank of England intervention at the long end, before 31 December. Absent those, this is expensive rather than broken.

consp.claim: That Britain is walking into an IMF bailout - that a 5.89 per cent thirty-year yield is the opening act of a rerun of 1976, when Chancellor Denis Healey went to the Fund and came back with conditions.
consp.spread: Mainstream enough to be quoted and fringe enough to be a meme at the same time. Liz Truss - whose own 49-day tenure is the reference everyone reaches for - publicly warned the rout could force Labour into emergency spending cuts, 'bond vigilante' commentary is back across financial media, and the harder version on X and in UK finance subreddits runs straight to sterling collapse and an IMF programme.
consp.read: The mechanism being described is real and the endgame is not established, which is the standard pattern for this genre. What is checkable: credit-derivative markets show little concern about a British default, which is precisely the instrument that would move first if solvency were the question rather than price. The 1976 analogy also imports a detail people forget - Britain went to the Fund under a fixed-ish exchange-rate regime with a sterling crisis, and a floating currency changes the mechanism materially. The honest distinction is between EXPENSIVE and BROKEN: 2022 was a solvency scare transmitted through pension-fund margin calls in days, while this is a grind driven by supply and inflation expectations, and grinds historically resolve through slower fiscal adjustment.

angles.effect: pay - fixed products are priced off gilt yields and reprice within weeks
pays - every basis point at the long end narrows the headroom the October Budget has to work with
gain - a 5.89 per cent long risk-free rate improves funding ratios for anyone holding long liabilities, which is the underdiscussed half of this story

angles.party: The 'it is the Iran war' framing
angles.effect: deflects - it converts a domestic fiscal choice into an external shock for which nobody in London can be blamed

dec.kill: Whether US and German long yields move with the gilt. If they do, this is a global duration repricing; if the gilt moves alone, it is a UK fiscal-credibility problem wearing a war costume.

watch: Saudi crude export loadings at Ras Tanura and Yanbu. This is the kill criterion on today's lead card. If loadings hold at recent volumes over the next fortnight, Tuesday was a refining and casualty event that the market priced as a supply event - and the $2 on Brent decays.

Impact bearings and recovered airframes from Abha, Najran and Jazan. This is the checkable kernel under the 'Iran targeted it, the Houthis signed it' claim now circulating. In 2019 the geometry broke the Houthi claim within months; here the targets are within Houthi range, so the geometry may confirm rather than break it. Either way it resolves in weeks.

Brent's CLOSE, every day to 24 September. Eight-tenths of one per cent from the $100 barrier with eleven sessions left, this is the observable that resolves GEO-009 and delivers this board its first Brier score in 31 open questions. The question resolves on closes, not intraday prints - which is worth 14 percentage points of survival probability on its own.

Whether US and German thirty-year yields track the gilt. If the long end repriced globally today, Britain is a passenger; if the gilt moved alone at 5.89 per cent, the war framing is covering a domestic fiscal problem. This is the cleanest single test on the plumbing card.

The $30bn reciprocal tariff-cut package. A published list, a Federal Register notice or a joint statement before 24 September converts the summit from a photograph into a transaction and would justify a further cut to GEO-007. Silence through the visit means the truce is drifting on inertia, which is a different and weaker thing.
lesson: Today's lesson is about proxies, and it explains why this board refused to raise its Iran forecast on a day when Iranian-aligned forces set Saudi oil sites on fire. When a state fights through someone else's army, it is buying a specific product: deniability. Idean Salehyan's work on the delegation of war to non-state groups sets out the trade - the sponsor gets cheapness and a plausible shrug, and pays for it with a principal-agent problem, because the proxy has its own war aims and can drag the sponsor somewhere it did not choose to go. Thomas Schelling's companion idea is that the ambiguity is not a bug: an attack nobody can cleanly attribute is a threat that is hard to answer without escalating first, which is why the wrapper is worth paying for. The base rate is where this stops being theory. On 14 September 2019, drones and cruise missiles knocked 5.7 million barrels a day - half of Saudi output - out of Abqaiq and Khurais; the Houthis claimed it, Washington publicly blamed Iran, UN monitors later found the Houthis could not have done it, and the American response was a troop deployment and sanctions, not a strike on Iran. So here is the discipline the lesson yields, and it is testable: attribution is not a trigger, ownership is. Watch whether anything hits an ASSET the United States must answer for - a US-flagged hull, an American casualty - because that, not the size of the fire in Jazan, is the variable that has historically moved American decisions.

quiz.q: Iranian-aligned forces set fire to Saudi oil facilities, and this board did NOT raise its forecast of a renewed US or Israeli strike campaign on Iran. What is the stated reason?
options: Because the attack was too small to matter to oil markets
Because in 2019 a far larger attack on Saudi oil - Abqaiq, half the kingdom's output - produced no American strike on Iran
Because the Houthis are not connected to Iran in any way
Because the US has publicly ruled out further strikes on Iran
quiz.why: The base rate is the discipline. Abqaiq removed 5.7 million barrels a day, was blamed on Iran by Washington, and produced a troop deployment and sanctions - not a strike. Damage to Saudi assets has historically not been the trigger; damage to American ones has, which is why this board's CRITICAL gate is a struck US-flagged hull or an American death rather than a burning refinery.

quiz.q: The brief says the Jazan complex is the asset that converts a Yemeni grievance into a global price. Why Jazan specifically rather than the size of any fire?
options: Because Jazan is where most Saudi crude is loaded for export
Because it is a 400,000 b/d refinery, about a tenth of Aramco's net refining capacity, and the world is short conversion capacity rather than crude
Because it is the closest facility to Iran
Because Jazan produces most of Saudi Arabia's electricity
quiz.why: A barrel of crude is not a usable product. The binding constraint in this cycle is the capacity to turn crude into diesel, so hitting a refinery bites harder per unit of damage than hitting a wellhead. Crude exports load at Ras Tanura and Yanbu, hundreds of miles from anything struck on Tuesday - which is why the brief's kill criterion is loadings, not fires.

quiz.q: Russia paused strikes on Kyiv for exactly the 72 hours that US envoys were in the region, then fired 166 drones. What does the brief say that timing reveals?
options: That Russia is running out of missiles and needed to reload
That Moscow can switch the air campaign on and off at will, which indicates confidence rather than exhaustion
That the pause was imposed on Russia by the United States
That Ukraine's air defences were down during the visit
quiz.why: A truce whose duration matches an itinerary to the hour is a scheduling accommodation, not a de-escalation - and the precision is itself the information. Fortna's finding is that ceasefires without monitors, guarantors or a demilitarised separation fail at high rates, and this arrangement had none of the three, which is why the 30-day ceasefire forecast was cut rather than raised.

quiz.q: The brief argues that stablecoins and the Fed's bill programme cannot fix Britain's 5.89 per cent thirty-year yield. What is the mechanism?
options: Because those programmes create demand for SHORT paper - bills - so the bid concentrates at the front of the curve and the long end is left to private buyers
Because the Bank of England is prohibited from buying gilts
Because stablecoins are illegal in the United Kingdom
Because thirty-year debt is not sold at auction
quiz.why: Tokenised dollar claims have to be backed by something short and liquid, which means Treasury bills. That manufactures a bid at the front end and does nothing for thirty-year duration, which is left to pension funds, insurers and price-sensitive foreigners who charge for inflation risk. Hence the brief's line that the long end is the leg no monetary innovation repairs.

quiz.q: CRITICAL THINKING. A widely circulated report puts transshipment - Chinese goods relabelled through third countries - at up to $303bn. Which observable best tests that CLAIM?
options: Whether the total Chinese trade surplus keeps rising
Whether more governments publicly endorse the report
Whether the rerouting rate holds up when customs data are matched WITHIN individual firms rather than at the product level
Whether Vietnam's exports to the US grew faster than its exports elsewhere
quiz.why: The size of the number depends almost entirely on how coarsely you match the data. Academic work found about 16.5 per cent of US-bound Vietnamese exports looked rerouted at the national product level, 6.5 per cent within provinces, and 1.7 per cent within individual firms - meaning aggregation was mistaking one company's genuine production for another's rerouting. The claim is checkable, and the check is firm-level matching.

sections.t: US diesel set an all-time record this week at $5.820 a gallon, and the crack spread — the refiner's fee for turning crude into something an engine can burn — printed an all-time $108 a barrel while Brent sat at an unremarkable $96. In the same week US missiles reportedly struck a tanker at Iran's Kharg Island anchorage, and Ukrainian drones held Russian refinery runs at 3.6m barrels a day, the lowest since May 2002.

Crude — the thing everyone photographs and embargoes — is behaving; refined product is not. A $108 crack means the market will pay more to convert a barrel than the barrel is worth: a fact about cokers and hydrotreaters, not about oil. Name the mechanism — the conversion bottleneck. The binding constraint is never the abundant input but the narrow step in the middle, which cannot be built on the timescale of a war or an election.

sections.h: Deep history I — Rockefeller never wanted the oil
sections.t: John D. Rockefeller owned almost no wells. He owned the refineries of Cleveland, and what he did with them in 1871 is the founding text of chokepoint economics. Tom Scott of the Pennsylvania Railroad chartered the South Improvement Company, and Rockefeller's terms inside it were breathtaking: the Erie, New York Central and Pennsylvania would pay the SIC a rebate of $1.06 on every barrel it shipped — and a drawback of $1.06 on every barrel shipped by refiners outside the club. He was paid when his rivals did business. The charter was repealed that April before a single transaction cleared, and Ida Tarbell's exposé later finished the job — but the insight outlived the scandal: crude is worthless until someone converts and moves it, and whoever owns the narrow step prices the wide one.

sections.h: Deep history II — the war decided at the still
sections.t: The largest test of this proposition was the Allied air war, fought inside the alliance before it was fought over Germany. Arthur Harris of RAF Bomber Command believed in punishment: burn the cities, break the will. Carl Spaatz and Arthur Tedder pushed what Harris dismissed as panacea targets — oil. Germany had almost no crude. It had Bergius hydrogenation, synthetic fuel pressed from coal at Leuna, Pölitz and Brüx, plants too enormous to hide. The oil plan began in May 1944. Leuna alone absorbed 22 raids, 6,552 bomber sorties and 18,328 tons of bombs across a year, behind Europe's heaviest flak concentration. It worked anyway. German synthetic output fell from a peak of 316,000 tons a month to 107,000 in June 1944 and 17,000 by September. Aviation gasoline — the specific fraction, not oil in general — went from 175,000 tons in April to 5,000 in September: 97% gone in five months. From May 1944 Germany consumed more than it produced every month, and the stockpile was gone in six.

sections.h: Deep history II — the fuel, not the factories
sections.t: The detail that makes it unforgettable: over the same period Albert Speer drove German tank and aircraft PRODUCTION to its wartime peak. The Reich ended 1944 with more airframes than it could fly and more panzers than it could move — the factories were fine and the fuel was not. The US Strategic Bombing Survey — written by people with every reason to praise bombing in general — judged the oil and transport campaigns decisive and the city campaign not. Japan lost the same way: the July 1941 freeze is remembered as an oil embargo, but the fatal shortage was 100-octane aviation gasoline, a conversion capability Japan could not build.

sections.h: Deep history III — how the West stopped building stills
sections.t: Now the slow part. The last greenfield major refinery built in the United States was Marathon's Garyville, Louisiana: built 1973-76, online 1977, still running at 596,000 barrels a day. Fifty years, no new plants — and the base is now shrinking: about 132 operable refineries in January 2025 against more than 300 in 1981, with roughly 1.235m b/d of distillation capacity removed in seven recent closures and conversions, over 6.5% of the total. All of it while shale made America the largest crude producer in history at 13.86m b/d. The country built the well and stopped building the still. The capacity emigrated rather than vanished — Jamnagar runs 1.24m b/d, Dangote opened at 650,000 and plans 1.4m, China kept building — so the toll moved east and south, to jurisdictions happy to buy discounted sanctioned crude and sell the product back to the people imposing the sanctions.

sections.h: The pattern — and where it breaks
sections.t: In all three cases the scarce thing is the transformation, and transformation capacity is inelastic over any politically relevant horizon: a new crude supplier takes a fortnight, a new hydrocracker takes five years and a billion dollars. Ukraine is now running the 1944 oil plan at a ten-thousandth of the cost, a drone flying 1,550km to Omsk doing what 6,552 B-17 sorties did to Leuna — Pape's denial thesis tested live. It breaks against me here: Germany had no crude and no neutral supplier, Russia has both, and a 24-year low in refining has not stopped Pokrovsk.

sections.h: The adjudication — Yergin and Blas vs Chris Miller
sections.t: THE ADJUDICATION — YERGIN AND BLAS versus CHRIS MILLER Yergin and Blas hold that energy chokepoints self-heal — inventories, bypass and rerouting absorb shocks forecast to be fatal — and they have been right about the barrel, Brent at $96 in a war that curtailed over 11m b/d. Chris Miller's Chip War argues the opposite for inputs that are not fungible: no reserve of fabs, no bypass for EUV, a decade to rebuild. The evidence splits them by step. Yergin and Blas won the crude argument; the crack is the market announcing the win does not survive one step downstream, because there is no strategic reserve of cokers — the US holds hundreds of millions of barrels of crude in the SPR and about a million barrels of distillate in the Northeast reserve, having stockpiled the input it cannot burn. Miller's case is still weaker in oil than in silicon: diesel is shippable in a way a fab's output is not, so refining heals in 12-24 months rather than 12-24 days.

OECD gasoline demand is in structural decline as EVs scale; diesel and jet demand are not, because trucks, ships, aircraft, mining and data-centre backup have no substitute. But a refinery makes every cut at once, so the economics that close Western refineries — falling gasoline — destroy the distillate capacity nobody meant to lose. A trap, not a cycle; confidence high. The bolder call, near 60%: by the mid-2030s the US is at once the world's largest crude exporter and a chronic net importer of middle distillates, and that buys a strategic PRODUCT reserve — legislated storage of diesel and jet, enacted after a winter shortage rather than before one. What keeps this honest is GEO-026: does the US diesel crack settle below $45 before 15 December 2026? It sits at 35%, so the house is 65% on regime rather than outage — and if the crack mean-reverts on the 2022 schedule, this is an elegant story about a spike, published as a miss.
